newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch still aim for mid-June EU treaty reform.
newsitem.headline: Dutch still aim for mid-June EU treaty reform.

text.p: A third of the way through its six-month European Union presidency, the Netherlands faces a daunting task to meet its promise of brokering treaty reforms to take the bloc's 370 million citizens into the 21st century.

After a rash of diplomatic gaffes -- upsetting the bloc's southern members hoping to join the exclusive single currency club and casting doubt on Turkey's EU membership credentials -- officials are putting a lid on public statements.
Behind the scenes, however, activity is frantic.
Diplomats are struggling to keep the inter-governmental conference (IGC) -- a wholesale review of the EU's unofficial "constitution" -- on track for meaningful reforms by mid-June.

Regular meetings of the IGC negotiating group, chaired by the Dutch, who favour letting countries forge ahead in some areas at different speeds, have broached vexed issues like flexibility and decision-making procedures but have made little headway on them.

One Dutch diplomat said defensively that talks on controversial issues, such as Qualified Majority Voting and flexibility, had advanced and not been railroaded by the spectre of British elections, due by May.
"We're not just waiting for the British to have their election. It's not just a British problem."

But Jan-Coen van Elburg, research associate at the Hague-based Clingendael Institute for International Relations, sees the election hobbling the pace of the IGC talks, with several states happy to use the forthcoming British ballot as an excuse to delay showing their own hands in the IGC negotiations.
"The focus on Britain hides the fact that other countries also have problems with extending qualified majority voting in certain areas," he said.

In Britain, neither the ruling Conservatives, sharply divided over the EU, nor the new-look Labour Party, out of office since 1979, favour erosion in the power of the national veto. Several other states share this view.

Diplomats say it is too early to judge the Dutch presidency, but note signs of movement on lesser issues, such as compromise deals on European Investment Bank loans and the likelihood of tangible progress in the fight against organised crime.
"The bulk of...meetings is still to be held. We are gathering speed," said one Dutch official.

Meanwhile the EMU juggernaut rolls on, threatening to overshadow other key issues, with talk of "stopping the clock" on economic and monetary union to give Germany, saddled with rising unemployment and a faltering economy, time to qualify.
Last week Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo warned that EMU postponement would risk damaging the process of EU integration.

"If you had to postpone EMU...there is a chance (its) prospects...would become diluted and that could lead to signs of disintegration...we could indeed go backwards in the process of coming closer together," he said.
His remark prompted Prime Minister Wim Kok to state publicly that the chances of EMU being postponed were, however, minimal.
Foreign relations, too, have at times been strained.
Van Mierlo caused consternation in Ankara when he said it was time Europe came clean on why it found it difficult to embrace Turkey as a prospective member.
Van Elburg said other partners had criticized the Dutch for being too open, objecting to information made public on the presidency's Internet site.

And in another diplomatic faux-pas, Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm advised certain countries to take their time preparing for EMU, but his comments were interpreted as a slap to Spain and Portugal. Again, remedial action was needed.
"The reaction was fierce and the Dutch are very much afraid that kind of reaction will come through in the IGC talks, too," van Elburg said.
"The Dutch want to avoid any dissent over EMU seeping into the IGC negotiations. They want to make the IGC a success, so they will try to put all the EMU discussions behind a curtain."
There has been little to date to alter the perception that, despite large doses of pragmatism and goodwill, the Dutch have a huge task to push through real reforms to the Maastricht Treaty.
"Although the chances have grown that there will be a treaty (of Amsterdam), it's likely to be only a minimal success as far as the content is concerned," Van Elburg said.
